## Prior to running any code

Please download the data from
<https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/stefanoleone992/mutual-funds-and-etfs>,
and store the file within a data/ folder in the working directory. If
the data is already stored then please skip this step.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(car)
library(writexl)
source('tools.R')
```

# 1. Load and clean the data

```{r clean-data}
columns <- c(
  "fund_return_ytd",
  "fund_annual_report_net_expense_ratio",
  "total_net_assets",
  "inception_date",
  "asset_stocks",
  "asset_bonds",
  "annual_holdings_turnover",
  "fund_price_earning_ratio",
  "fund_sector_technology"
)

funds <- rbind(
  transform(read.csv("data/ETFs.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))[columns],
            etf_indicator = 1),
  transform(read.csv("data/MutualFunds.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))[columns],
            etf_indicator = 0)
)

funds <- funds |>
  mutate(
    fund_age_years = as.numeric(as.Date("2021-01-01") - as.Date(inception_date)) / 365.25
  ) |>
  filter(fund_age_years > 0) |>
  mutate(
    pe_reported = as.integer(!is.na(fund_price_earning_ratio)),
    pe_centered_when_reported = {
      pe <- fund_price_earning_ratio
      median_pe <- median(pe, na.rm = TRUE)
      ifelse(is.na(pe), median_pe, pe) - median_pe
    }
  ) |>
  select(-inception_date)

# Use the two P/E terms in the model and keep the raw P/E in funds for the audit.
model_data <- select(funds, -fund_price_earning_ratio)
model_data <- model_data[complete.cases(model_data), ]
```

## Sample and missingness audit

```{r part2-eda-sample, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
fund_type <- function(indicator) {
  factor(indicator, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Mutual fund", "ETF"))
}

sample_counts <- rbind(
  "Eligible before complete filtering" = table(fund_type(funds$etf_indicator)),
  "Main model sample" = table(fund_type(model_data$etf_indicator)),
  "P/E reported in model sample" = table(fund_type(
    model_data$etf_indicator[model_data$pe_reported == 1L]
  ))
)

retained_pct <- round(100 * sample_counts[2, ] / sample_counts[1, ], 1)

# Count missing values and count which fields cause loss.
# Seperately for etf and mutual fund.
missing_counts <- sapply(
  split(funds[c(setdiff(columns, "inception_date"), "fund_age_years")],
        fund_type(funds$etf_indicator)),
  function(group) colSums(is.na(group))
)

knitr::kable(cbind(sample_counts, Total = rowSums(sample_counts)))
knitr::kable(rbind("Eligible observations retained (%)" = retained_pct))
knitr::kable(missing_counts)
```

# 2. Fit the basic model

```{r regression}
model <- lm(fund_return_ytd ~ total_net_assets +
    fund_age_years + asset_stocks + asset_bonds +
    annual_holdings_turnover +
    fund_sector_technology + pe_reported + pe_centered_when_reported +
    fund_annual_report_net_expense_ratio * etf_indicator,
  data = model_data
)
fitted_data <- model.frame(model) # Extracting rows-variables used by lm()
```

# 5. Exploratory checks

## Removing most influential fund from model

```{r}
most_influential <- which.max(checks$diagnostics$cooks)
model_ex <- lm(formula = formula(model), data = model_data[-most_influential, ])
summary(model_ex)
```

### Explanation

The most influential point by cooks distance of 2.55 above course cutoff of 0.95.
Removing that observation changes the interaction term (fee x fund type) coefficient
from approximatedly 0.27 to -2.84. It also becomes significant with p-value of 0.004
where previously 0.637.

The new model's R^2 values and RSS largely remain unchanged due to large sampling.

Can we justify removing this point?
Not entirely. This point corresponds to fund with ticker BIZD aka "American Balanced
Fund". It exceeds all 3 cuttoffs. For this observation, we see unusually high expense
ratio but potentially valid given the portfolios underlying composition of the
portfolio, but this is they key factor giving it high leverage.

Independently checking this point we see results match the fund profile thus it can 
be excluded as erroneous data. It's studentized residuals are large, so the model 
just fits its returns poorly.

### What about other influential points?

Checking commonly flagged observations for exceeding cutoffs, several points exceeded
2 cutoffs and even more exceeded 1. ETFs were more commonly flagged at a 56% rate 
compared to 16% of mutual funds. Most flagged points were funds categoriezed into:
- Equity precious metal
- Real estate
- Energy
- Leveraged Equities
- Chinese regional funds

Broadly speaking, each type of fund either outperformed or underperformed due to
underlying market conditions. Keep in mind year 2021 was post-covid recovery.
* Leveraged assets should always performed unexpectedly due to their nature.
* Oil demand recovered faster than supply after economy opened up pushing higher prices.
* Rising rates and precious metals were correlated.

## Verifying assumptions

### Trial transformations based on plots

Using the **same observations**, we refit the model using appropriate transformations.

```{r fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
log_assets_model <- lm(
  fund_return_ytd ~ . - total_net_assets + log(total_net_assets) +
    fund_annual_report_net_expense_ratio:etf_indicator,
  data = model_data, na.action = na.fail
)

sqrt_return_model <- lm(
  sqrt(1 + fund_return_ytd) ~ . - total_net_assets + sqrt(total_net_assets) +
    fund_annual_report_net_expense_ratio:etf_indicator,
  data = model_data, na.action = na.fail
)

log_return_model <- lm(
  log(1 + fund_return_ytd) ~ . - total_net_assets + log(total_net_assets) +
    fund_annual_report_net_expense_ratio:etf_indicator,
  data = model_data, na.action = na.fail
)
```

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}
# Residual and QQ plot comparison
model_plots(model)$residual_comparison(title = "Original model")
model_plots(log_assets_model)$residual_comparison(title = "Log assets")
model_plots(sqrt_return_model)$residual_comparison(title = "Square-root return and assets")
model_plots(log_return_model)$residual_comparison(title = "Log return and assets")

model_plots(model)$residuals_vs_predictors("total_net_assets")
model_plots(log_assets_model)$residuals_vs_predictors("log(total_net_assets)")
model_plots(sqrt_return_model)$residuals_vs_predictors("sqrt(total_net_assets)")
model_plots(log_return_model)$residuals_vs_predictors("log(total_net_assets)")
```

Note about transformations- potentially inconclusive

### Applying Box-Cox profile

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}
# Turn returns positive by adding 1
gross_model <- update(model, I(1 + fund_return_ytd) ~ .)

# Run the boxcox on the strictly positive model
bc <- MASS::boxcox(gross_model, lambda = seq(-2, 4, by = 0.05))

# Find power at highest point and draw it
lambda <- bc$x[which.max(bc$y)]
abline(v = lambda, col = "red", lty = 2)
lambda

# Get 95% plausible range of cutoff values
cutoff <- max(bc$y) - qchisq(0.95, df = 1) / 2
lambda_ci <- range(bc$x[bc$y >= cutoff])
c(estimate = lambda, lower = lambda_ci[1], upper = lambda_ci[2])
```

Note about box-cox. Also potentially inconclusive aka no transformation required
